issues.legal_issue: A civil court at trial must accept the Land Tribunal’s decision on a referred question of tenant status, while an appellate court may review the resulting finding.
material_facts: The defendant claimed that an oral lease made him a tenant.
The trial court referred the tenant-status question to the Land Tribunal, which found that the defendant was a tenant.
The trial court rejected the Tribunal’s finding and decided that the defendant was not a tenant.
The High Court considered the tenant-status question and upheld the decree for possession.
issues.conclusion: The trial court had no jurisdiction to record a finding contrary to the Tribunal’s decision on the referred question. The appellate court was, however, entitled to examine that finding, and the High Court did so.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 125(3)–(6) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, the civil court refers a tenant-status question to the Land Tribunal and, at trial, must accept the Tribunal’s decision. Under Section 125(6), that decision is treated as part of the civil court’s finding for appeal, so the appellate court may review it as it may review other findings.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_tenant_status: A civil suit or other civil proceeding involves a question about whether a person has tenant status.
predicates.tribunal_decided_referred_question: The Land Tribunal decided the tenant-status question referred to it by the civil court.
predicates.tribunal_returned_decision: The Land Tribunal returned its decision to the civil court for the proceeding to continue.

issues.definition: When a civil proceeding includes a tenant-status question decided by the Tribunal, the trial court accepts that decision, while an appellate court may review the resulting finding.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court need not refer an asserted tenant-status question to the Land Tribunal when the plea is not bona fide and legally sustainable.
material_facts: The defendant asserted that an oral lease made him a tenant from 1971.
The asserted tenancy began after the statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies had taken effect.
The defendant argued before the trial court that a reference was unnecessary because the alleged lease was prohibited, but later relied on the Tribunal’s finding in his favour.
issues.conclusion: A reference was not required merely because the defendant asserted tenant status; the claim was legally untenable, so the civil court was not obliged to refer it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 125(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act requires a reference only when the tenant-status question genuinely or legally arises. The Court relied on Keshava Bhat v. Subraya Bhat, Muhammad Haji v. Kunhuni Nair, and Sundaram v. Mohammed Koya for the proposition that an untenable or merely delaying plea need not be referred. It distinguished Sankaranarayanan Potti v. K. Sreedevi, explaining that the scope of the word “arises” was not decided there.

predicates.civil_proceeding_involves_tenant_status: A civil suit or other civil proceeding involves an asserted question of tenant status.
predicates.party_asserts_tenant_status: A party claims that they have tenant status in relation to the property.
predicates.plea_has_no_remote_legal_basis: The circumstances show that there is not even a remote possibility that the tenant-status plea could legally be upheld.

issues.definition: If a party asserts tenant status in a civil proceeding but the plea has no remote legal basis, the civil court need not refer the question to the Tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: A tenancy created after a statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies has taken effect is invalid and cannot establish a right to remain in possession.
material_facts: The defendant claimed that an oral lease made him a tenant from 1971.
The alleged lease was created after the statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies had taken effect.
The plaintiff sought recovery of possession, and the defendant relied on the alleged tenancy to resist that claim.
issues.conclusion: The alleged tenancy was invalid, and no court could find that it gave the defendant tenant status. A remand was unnecessary, and the decree for possession was properly upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 74 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act prohibits the creation of a tenancy after the Act’s commencement and makes a tenancy created in contravention of that prohibition invalid. In light of that absolute bar and the undisputed timing of the alleged lease, the Court held that remand would serve only to prolong the litigation.

predicates.property_possession_suit_involves_tenant: A suit seeking possession of property is resisted on the basis of a claimed tenancy.
predicates.alleged_tenancy_created_after_prohibitio: The alleged tenancy was created after a statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies had taken effect.

issues.definition: When a possession suit is resisted by a claimed tenancy created after the prohibition took effect, that tenancy is invalid and cannot establish tenant status.
